exercises.name: Two-ball dribbling series
exercises.note: Alternating, crossover and low-pound combos at game speed. Keep the eyes up the entire time so the hands learn to work without needing visual feedback on the ball.

exercises.name: Cone attack + finishes
exercises.note: Change of pace into euro-step, floater and reverse layups. The goal is deceleration control — sell the burst, then decide the finish only after the last defender has committed.

exercises.name: Tight-space handle work
exercises.note: In-and-out, behind-back and hesitation in a 1m box. Working in a tiny footprint forces the ball to stay low and close, which is exactly what survives real ball pressure.

exercises.name: Contact finishing (pad)
exercises.note: Absorb a bump, finish through with both hands. A coach or partner delivers the pad contact mid-air so the body learns to stay balanced and convert even when hit.

exercises.name: Form shooting close-out
exercises.note: One-hand then two, locking the release point. Start close to the rim and only step back once the elbow, wrist snap and follow-through are repeating identically.

exercises.name: Pull-up mid-range series
exercises.note: One-dribble pull-ups off both directions. Emphasize a hard, low first dribble into a balanced jump-stop — most missed pull-ups start with sloppy footwork, not a bad release.

exercises.name: Step-back threes
exercises.note: Create space, land balanced, hold follow-through. Land with the shoulders square to the rim rather than fading away, so the shot stays repeatable under a real closeout.

exercises.name: Catch-and-shoot 3s
exercises.note: Off relocation and screens, on the move. High volume here builds a rhythm that survives fatigue — the shot has to look the same on rep 200 as it did on rep 1.

exercises.name: Lateral bounds
exercises.note: Stick the landing, build hip stability. A full 2-3 second hold on each landing teaches the joint to absorb force instead of just reacting to it.

exercises.name: Resisted sprints
exercises.note: Band or sled for explosive first step. The added resistance forces a lower, more powerful drive phase — that's the difference between beating a defender by a step or not at all.

exercises.name: Ladder + reaction cuts
exercises.note: Fast feet into a coach-called cut. The unpredictable cue trains the nervous system to react to a defender's actual movement, not a memorized pattern.

exercises.name: Anti-rotation core (Pallof)
exercises.note: Brace the trunk for finishing through contact. A stable core is what lets a smaller guard absorb a hit at the rim without losing the shot or drawing the offensive foul.

exercises.name: Trap-bar deadlift
exercises.note: Lower-body power without heavy spinal load. The neutral grip lets guards build real posterior-chain strength while keeping the lower back fresh for the next day's on-court work.

exercises.name: Bulgarian split squat
exercises.note: Single-leg strength and balance. Most basketball moves happen off one leg, so this closes the gap between weight-room strength and strength that actually shows up in a crossover or finish.

exercises.name: Weighted pull-ups
exercises.note: Upper-back strength for finishing and defense. A strong back and lats help a guard hold their ground on post switches and absorb contact on drives without getting knocked off-balance.

exercises.name: Nordic hamstring curls
exercises.note: Hamstring health, sprint protection. This is the single best-studied exercise for cutting soft-tissue injury risk, which matters most for guards logging heavy sprint mileage every game.

exercises.name: Jab-series into pull-up
exercises.note: Sell the jab, rise into a balanced jumper. The jab step has to look identical whether it's a fake or a real drive, or defenders stop respecting it after the first rep.

exercises.name: Iso attack finishes
exercises.note: Face-up, one dribble, finish over length. Focus on a high release point at the rim so the shot can't be reached by a longer, help-side defender rotating late.

exercises.name: Mid-post turnarounds
exercises.note: Footwork into fadeaway and up-and-under. Establish the pivot foot early and work both the baseline and middle counters so the move can't be scouted and shut down.

exercises.name: Transition pull-ups
exercises.note: Sprint the floor, decelerate, knock it down. The hard part isn't the shot, it's controlling the deceleration after a full-speed sprint — practice that braking mechanic specifically.

exercises.name: Guided form shooting
exercises.note: Fix the base, elbow and follow-through. Slow the motion down deliberately here — the goal is a mechanically identical shot every time, not volume for its own sake.

exercises.name: Catch-and-shoot 3s
exercises.note: Spot-up and off relocation. Vary the catch angle and footwork so the shot holds up whether the pass arrives on a stationary catch or on the move.

exercises.name: Movement 3s off screens
exercises.note: Come off tight, square and fire. Brush the screener's shoulder on the way by — separation from the defender matters more here than the shot itself.

exercises.name: Free throws under fatigue
exercises.note: After sprints, simulate late-game legs. The routine has to be automatic when the legs are heavy, since that's exactly the state free throws get shot in during the fourth quarter.

exercises.name: Depth jumps to box
exercises.note: Reactive power for finishing and blocks. The step-off height should be challenging but land clean — this trains the stretch-shortening cycle that powers a second jump for a block or putback.

exercises.name: Defensive slide circuit
exercises.note: Stay low, mirror, close out. Keep the hips below the shoulders throughout — standing up even slightly costs a full step of lateral quickness against a live ball-handler.

exercises.name: Med-ball rotational throws
exercises.note: Transfer power through the hips. This builds the same hip-to-shoulder sequencing used in a contested finish or a one-handed defensive strip.

exercises.name: Sprint-decel ladders
exercises.note: Control the stop to change direction. Most blown defensive assignments come from a slow deceleration, not a slow sprint — this drills the braking mechanic in isolation.

exercises.name: Back squat
exercises.note: Foundational lower-body strength. Keep this heavy but technically clean — it's the base that every explosive movement on the floor eventually draws from.

exercises.name: Weighted step-ups
exercises.note: Single-leg drive for finishing. Drive through the full foot rather than the toes, building the same push-off pattern used attacking a closeout.

exercises.name: Bench + row superset
exercises.note: Balanced upper-body push/pull. Matching push and pull volume protects the shoulder joint from the repetitive strain of thousands of shots over a season.

exercises.name: Shoulder & cuff prep
exercises.note: Keep the shooting shoulder durable. Light, high-rep band work here is prehab, not an afterthought — it's cheap insurance against the shoulder fatigue that quietly wrecks shooting form late in a season.

exercises.name: Mikan & reverse Mikan
exercises.note: Soft touch with both hands at the rim. Stay on the balls of the feet throughout — the drill is as much about foot rhythm around the basket as it is about the finish itself.

exercises.name: Post-move series
exercises.note: Drop step, jump hook, up-and-under. Catch with the pivot foot decided before the ball arrives, so the counter move is instant instead of telegraphed to the defense.

exercises.name: Short-roll decisions
exercises.note: Catch on the move, finish or kick. A coach reads the defense live and calls the coverage — the point is training the read, not memorizing which option comes next.

exercises.name: Face-up drive & floater
exercises.note: Attack a close-out from the elbow. One hard dribble should be enough to get to a floater window — extra dribbles just give the recovering defense time to contest.

exercises.name: Form-to-3 shooting
exercises.note: Extend the same stroke to the arc. Nothing changes about the mechanics from mid-range to three — only the legs work harder to deliver the same release point.

exercises.name: Pick-and-pop 3s
exercises.note: Screen, relocate, catch and shoot. Set the screen with real contact first — a soft screen means the guard never gets enough separation for the pop to be worth anything.

exercises.name: High-post passing reads
exercises.note: Hit cutters and shooters from the elbow. Catch with the head up so the read happens before the catch, not after — that split-second is what turns a good look into a great one.

exercises.name: Free throws
exercises.note: Repeatable routine, high volume. The exact same number of dribbles, same breath, same release every single time — consistency here compounds over an 82-game season.

exercises.name: Vertical contest jumps
exercises.note: Contest without fouling, land balanced. Straight up with the arms extended, not leaning into the shooter — that's the difference between an altered shot and a shooting foul.

exercises.name: Lateral drop-coverage
exercises.note: Slide with guards, recover to the rim. Stay in a low defensive stance the whole rep so the recovery step to the paint doesn't cost an extra beat of reaction time.

exercises.name: Rebound & outlet
exercises.note: Box out, secure, start the break. Find contact on the box-out before the ball even arrives — positioning wins boards far more often than a late, athletic recovery.

exercises.name: Hip mobility flow
exercises.note: Keep big hips loose and springy. A few unhurried minutes here protect the joints that carry the most load on a taller frame, and they pay off in defensive lateral quickness too.

exercises.name: Front squat
exercises.note: Posture and leg drive for post work. The upright torso this position demands directly mirrors the posture needed to hold ground on the block against a bigger defender.

exercises.name: Trap-bar jump
exercises.note: Explosive power off two feet. Reset fully between reps — this is about producing maximum force each jump, not grinding through fatigue.

exercises.name: Heavy carries
exercises.note: Core and grip strength for battles. Walking under load builds the same trunk stability and grip endurance needed to hold a post position against constant physical pressure.

exercises.name: Overhead press
exercises.note: Finishing strength through contact. Strong shoulders and triceps let a finish stay high and away from a shot-blocker's reach even when a defender is hanging on the arm.
